title: 004 — OpenAI Decisions API: fast, typed yes/no, choice and score answers
html:
004 — OpenAI Decisions API: fast, typed yes/no, choice and score answers

The one idea: The Decisions API is a separate OpenAI endpoint that answers fixed questions about text or an image and returns typed answers (a probability, a chosen option with confidence, or a score) instead of free text. OpenAI says it is about 10x faster than the Responses API and it bills input tokens only, so it fits classification, routing and checks inside an application.

Added 2026-10-07 · Public beta on 2026-10-06 by OpenAI (announced at DevDay, 29 Sep 2026)

1. What it is

POST /v1/decisions takes three fields:

  • model: only gpt-6-luna for now.
  • input: a text string, or user messages with text and images.
  • questions: an array of questions to answer about that input.

Each question has a type, a name and instructions. There are three types:

Type Use it for What comes back
predicate Is this condition true? probability from 0 to 1
choice Which of these fixed options fits? the choice, a confidence and per-option probabilities
score Where on an ordered scale does this sit? a score (probability-weighted), a confidence and probabilities

A model can also return a refusal answer.

2. Why it matters

Most applications that call an LLM for a decision (is this ticket urgent, which team owns it, does this photo show damage) do not need prose. They need a value they can branch on. Doing that with a chat or Responses call means prompt work to force a format, parsing that can fail, and paying for output tokens.

The Decisions API removes all three problems:

  • Typed output. The answer is already a number or a label.
  • Calibration. A probability or confidence lets code send uncertain cases to a person or a stronger model.
  • Cost and latency. It costs $0.10 per 1M input tokens, with no output or cache charges, and OpenAI says it is roughly 10x faster than the Responses API. That makes it practical to call inside a request path.

It is the same idea as Databricks ai_decide, but as a general API you can call from any service rather than from SQL over a governed table.

3. How it works

---
title: Decisions API in a request path
---
flowchart LR
    U["Incoming item<br/>(text or image)"] --> S["Your .NET service"]
    S --> D["POST /v1/decisions<br/>(gpt-6-luna)"]
    D --> A["answers[]<br/>probability / choice / score"]
    A --> T{"Above threshold?"}
    T -- yes --> X["Act automatically"]
    T -- no --> H["Human review<br/>or stronger model"]

Questions in one request are answered independently. If one decision depends on another (first classify, then score only some classes), make two calls.

4. How to use it

OpenAI's guide shows this request, which checks a product photo for damage:

{
  "model": "gpt-6-luna",
  "input": [{
    "role": "user",
    "content": [
      {"type": "input_text", "text": "Inspect the product in this photo."},
      {"type": "input_image", "image_url": "data:image/png;base64,[IMAGE_BASE64]"}
    ]
  }],
  "questions": [{
    "type": "predicate",
    "name": "visible_damage",
    "instructions": "Does the product have visible damage, such as a crack, tear, or dent? Ignore shadows and damage to the packaging."
  }]
}

The response:

{ "answers": [ { "type": "predicate", "name": "visible_damage", "probability": 0.92 } ] }

The same text-only call from C# with HttpClient:

using System.Net.Http.Json;

using var http = new HttpClient { BaseAddress = new Uri("https://api.openai.com/") };
http.DefaultRequestHeaders.Authorization =
    new("Bearer", Environment.GetEnvironmentVariable("OPENAI_API_KEY"));

var request = new
{
    model = "gpt-6-luna",
    input = ticketText,
    questions = new[]
    {
        new { type = "predicate", name = "is_outage",
              instructions = "Does the ticket report that a production system is down?" }
    }
};

using var response = await http.PostAsJsonAsync("v1/decisions", request);
response.EnsureSuccessStatusCode();
Console.WriteLine(await response.Content.ReadAsStringAsync());

The C# version follows the documented field names. Check the guide for the extra fields that choice and score questions need (their options or levels) before writing those.

In practice:

  • Keep the questions in configuration, versioned, so a change in wording is reviewed like code.
  • Store the probability with each decision. It lets you tune the threshold later from real data.
  • Log a sample of decisions and check them by hand every so often, because the model can drift between versions.

5. Trade-offs and limits

  • Beta. Fields and behaviour may change before GA, and only one model is supported.
  • Images must be inline base64 data URLs. HTTP links are not accepted, which adds payload size.
  • Not for generation. It does not write summaries or extract free text.
  • Pricing extras. Regional processing premiums and long-context multipliers apply on top of the base price.
  • Compliance. Zero Data Retention and HIPAA are available for eligible customers in the US and Europe regions. Check this before you send customer data.
  • Adopt now or wait? It is a good fit for new triage and routing features today. Moving an existing, working Responses-based classifier can wait for GA, unless cost or latency is the pain point.

6. Where it fits

  • LLM engineering and RAG: when a specialised call beats a general prompt.
  • Databricks ai_decide: the same pattern inside SQL.
  • GPT-6.1 Sol: the GPT-6 family that Luna belongs to.
  • API design: wrapping a vendor API behind your own interface.

7. Questions to test yourself

  1. Why is a predicate probability more useful to an application than a yes/no string?
  2. You need to classify a ticket and then score its urgency only if it is about billing. How many calls do you make, and why?
  3. What do you store with each decision so you can tune the threshold later?
  4. When would you keep a Responses API call instead of moving to the Decisions API?
